# Templates {.unnumbered}

The sixteen templates below are starting points to copy and edit. A, C, E, F, L, M and N work with any tool, and O works with any repository on GitHub. B, G and I are skills, stored as a `SKILL.md` file, a format that Claude Code, Codex and Gemini CLI all read, so they should need little change, except that B hands its checking step to the subagent in D. J and K are skills that also use Claude Code settings, such as `disable-model-invocation`, which other tools may not accept. D defines a subagent with Claude Code's settings, such as the list of tools it may use, and H combines a skill with two such subagents; both need rewriting for another tool, as does the Claude Code hook in P. None has been tested on a live module, so run each on a small example first. Each is also a file in the `templates/` folder of the repository.

### A. Module instruction file {#tpl-a}

Save as `MODULE.md`, or under the name your agent reads at the start of every session: `CLAUDE.md` in Claude Code, `AGENTS.md` in Codex, `GEMINI.md` in Gemini CLI. The examples come from an asset-pricing module; replace them, and delete any section that does not apply.

```text
# ECN000 Module Title

Standing instructions for the agent. Keep this file to one or two pages.
Replace every [bracket], delete the examples that do not apply, and put
detail for a single task (a rubric, a marking scheme) in its own file.

## Module facts
- Level [6], [15] credits, about [120] students, taught in [term 1].
- Prerequisites: [ECN000 Econometrics I]. Co-requisites: [none].
- Teaching: [10] lectures of [100] minutes, [10] tutorials, [5] computer labs.
- Module leader: [name]. Teaching assistants: [names, or see admin/staff.md].

## Learning outcomes
As approved in the module specification. Do not reword them.
1. [Estimate a linear factor model and test its restrictions.]
2. [...]
Every lecture plan, problem set and assessment says which outcomes it serves.

## What students know
- Assume: [linear algebra to eigenvalues; OLS and its asymptotic theory;
  Python with pandas, numpy and matplotlib].
- Do not assume: [maximum likelihood; matrix calculus; R or Stata].
- Where students usually struggle: [moving from moment conditions to the GMM
  objective; reading a table with clustered standard errors].

## Notation
- Returns r_t, excess returns r^e_t; logs lower case, levels upper case.
- Vectors bold lower case, matrices bold upper case; estimators carry a hat.
- E_t[.] is the expectation conditional on information at time t.
- Where this list is silent, follow [textbook], chapters [x-y].

## Software
- Python [3.12]. Packages pinned in requirements.txt; use no others.
- Every notebook runs from top to bottom in a fresh kernel before release.
- Lecture notes use lectures/template.tex and compile with latexmk.

## Folders and file names
- lectures/weekNN/: plan.md, notes.tex, slides.tex, figures/ with the script
  that produces each figure.
- problem-sets/psN/: questions.tex, solutions.tex, solve.py, data/.
- sources/: read-only. sources/third-party/ holds licensed material.
- assessment/: outside version control. Never shared, synced or uploaded.

## House style
- British spelling.
- One lecture is [100] minutes: at most [25] slides and [two] worked examples.
- Full rules: the lecture-style skill in .claude/skills/lecture-style/.

## Rules
- Never edit anything in sources/.
- Never supply a reference, fact or number that is not in sources/ or in code
  output. If something is missing, stop and list it.
- Every number in a solution, table or figure comes from a script that has
  been run.
- Compile or run every file before reporting it finished.
- No student work, marks or personal data in this folder.
- Commit before and after each task, with a message saying what changed and
  why. Never commit anything in assessment/.
- Ask before deleting a file or changing more than one week's material in a
  single task.

## Related files
- Coursework rubric: [assessment/coursework-rubric.md]. Read it only when
  working on marking or on the assessment.
- Module outline and schedule: admin/outline.md.

## Decisions log
One dated line per decision, newest last, so that settled questions are not reopened.
- 2026-11-26  Dropped the Kalman filter lecture; replaced by a second GMM lab.
- [date]  [decision, and the reason for it]
```

### B. Problem-set skill {#tpl-b}

Save as `.claude/skills/problem-set/SKILL.md`, with the checker from [template D](#tpl-d) in `.claude/agents/`. Run with `/problem-set week05`.

```text
---
name: problem-set
description: Draft a problem set with verified solutions for one week of the module.
---

Write a problem set for $ARGUMENTS.

1. Read CLAUDE.md, the lecture notes for that week, and two past problem sets
   in problem-sets/ as the standard for style and difficulty.
2. Propose a one-page plan: each question, the outcome it tests, the expected
   time, and whether it is mechanical, applied or stretch. Wait for approval.
3. Write questions.tex, solutions.tex and solve.py in a new folder.
4. Run solve.py. Take every number in solutions.tex from its output.
5. For derivations, verify each final expression symbolically or numerically.
6. Compile both .tex files and fix any errors.
7. Use the checker subagent on the new folder: it solves questions.tex
   without seeing solutions.tex, then compares. Do not change a solution
   to match the checker; list every disagreement for me to resolve.
8. Report: what was produced, what was verified and how, every disagreement
   the checker found, and anything you could not verify. List the stretch
   questions so that I can attempt them myself.

Do not reuse or paraphrase questions from textbooks in sources/.
```

### C. Marking notes to feedback {#tpl-c}

The feedback step from chapter 8, for one script or a folder of them. Use it only with a tool your university has approved for student work (chapter 10), and read every piece of feedback in full before it is released.

```text
I have marked one anonymised script and set the mark. Turn my marking notes
into written feedback for the student. Do not suggest, change or comment on
the mark.

Before writing
- If the notes or the script contain a name, student number or email
  address, stop and tell me. Do not write anything.
- If my notes say nothing about a rubric criterion, say so in your reply
  rather than filling the gap.

The feedback
- About [150-200] words, addressed to the student as "you", in British
  spelling.
- One or two sentences on what the work did well, taken from my notes.
- The [two] most important improvements, each tied to a named rubric
  criterion and to a specific place in the script (question, section or page).
- One concrete step the student can take in the next assessment.
- No praise or criticism that my notes do not support, no comparison with
  other students, no classification words ("first-class", "a solid 2:1"),
  and no mention of AI.

Use only what is in my notes and the rubric. Do not add observations of your
own, even where they seem obvious from the script.

Rubric (criteria and band descriptors):
[paste]

My notes:
[paste]

Reply with
1. The feedback, ready to paste.
2. Each sentence of the feedback with the note it comes from, so that I can
   check it.

For a batch: the folder [feedback/coursework1/] holds one notes file per
candidate number. Write one feedback file for each, named by candidate
number, and finish with a table counting the improvements raised under each
rubric criterion, for the cohort report.
```

### D. Independent checker {#tpl-d}

The session B of chapter 9, which solves the questions before it sees the solutions. Save as `.claude/agents/checker.md`. The `tools` line limits it to reading files.

```text
---
name: checker
description: Independently solves a problem set from the questions alone and reports disagreements with the official solutions. Use before any solutions are released.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob
---

You are checking a problem set for a university module. You will be told the
folder that holds it.

1. Read CLAUDE.md for the notation and for what students are assumed to know.
2. Read the questions file only. Do not open the solutions, the solution code
   or its output yet.
3. Solve every question yourself and show the working. You cannot run code:
   where a number needs computation, write the code you would run and mark
   the number as unconfirmed.
4. Only then read the official solutions and the output of the solution code.
5. Compare question by question. Treat two numbers as agreeing when they
   match to the precision the question asks for.

Report first a table:

| Question | Verdict | Your answer | Official answer | Likely source of any difference |

where the verdict is agree, disagree, or unconfirmed (needs computation).

Then list, each with the question number and the wording concerned:
- questions that can be read in more than one way;
- questions that can be answered without the intended method;
- questions harder than their stated level or time, and the step that makes
  them so;
- solutions that give the right number with a wrong or missing
  interpretation;
- notation that differs from CLAUDE.md.

Do not edit files or run code; your output is the report.
```

### E. Student-facing AI statement {#tpl-e}

The statement from chapter 11, for the module outline. The permitted uses are an example; set your own for each assessment, and fill the bracketed points from your school's policy.

```text
Use of AI tools in ECN000 [Module title], [academic year]

This statement says what use of AI tools is permitted in each part of the
module. Where an assessment brief says something different, the brief applies.

| Activity | Weight | AI use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Problem sets and labs | not assessed | Any use |
| Coursework | 40% | Debugging code and checking grammar only |
| Exam | 60% | None (invigilated) |

Problem sets and labs (not assessed). Any use is permitted. You will learn
more by attempting each question before asking a tool, and the exam tests the
same methods without one.

Coursework (40%). You may use AI tools to find and fix errors in your code
and to check spelling and grammar. You may not use them to:
- write or rewrite any part of the interpretation, discussion or conclusion;
- choose the method, the specification or the data;
- produce tables or figures that your own code did not generate.

Declaration. End your submission with a short paragraph naming each tool you
used and what you used it for, for example: "I used [tool] to find an
indexing error in the code for Table 2. I did not use AI tools for any other
part of this work." [State how a missing declaration is treated.]

Responsibility. You are responsible for everything you submit, including
errors, invented references and copied material introduced by a tool.

Verification. Any student may be asked to explain their submission in a short
conversation with the module team. [State how students are selected and how
the conversation is used, following school policy.]

Exam (60%). Invigilated. No AI tools.

Access. The university provides [tool] to all students at no cost through
[link]. No assessment in this module requires a paid subscription.

Questions and mistakes. If you are unsure whether a use is permitted, ask
[name or forum] before you submit. Use beyond this statement is handled
under the university's academic misconduct procedure [link]. Report any
mistake you find in the module material through [channel].

How AI was used in preparing this module. Lecture notes and problem sets were
drafted with an AI coding agent from my own notes. I checked every part, and
every number in a solution comes from code that was run. All marks are set by
the teaching team. [State any use in feedback, for example: "Written feedback
is expanded from the marker's own notes with an approved AI tool, and the
marker reads it in full before release."]
```

### F. Assessment stress test {#tpl-f}

The stress test from chapter 7, as a checklist and a record sheet. Copy it into `assessment/` for each test, and keep the completed sheets so that next year's result can be compared with this year's.

```text
# Assessment stress test

Assessment: [name, weight]            Date: [date]
Tool and model: [name and version]    Tested by: [name]
Keep this record in assessment/, outside version control.

## Before
- [ ] A fresh session in an empty folder outside the module, with none of
      the module's files and no instruction file
- [ ] The folder holds exactly what a student receives: brief, data,
      reading list
- [ ] Rubric and marking scheme to hand
- [ ] Past scripts for blind marking, only if your university permits
      their use for this purpose

## Attempt 1: one pass
Send this prompt as written:
  "Complete this assessment as a student would. The brief and any data are
  in this folder. Produce the full submission in the required format."
- [ ] Submission saved as attempt-1

## Attempt 2: one round of follow-up
In the same session, send one follow-up of the kind a student would, such as:
  "Check that the code runs and that every number in the text matches the
  output, then make the discussion more critical."
- [ ] Submission saved as attempt-2

## Marking
- [ ] Both attempts marked against the rubric, mixed with [n] other scripts
      and marked blind where possible

| Criterion | Weight | Attempt 1 | Attempt 2 | Typical student | What the agent got wrong |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [criterion] | [%] | | | | |
| [criterion] | [%] | | | | |
| Total | 100 | | | | |

"Typical student" is the average mark on that criterion in recent years.
A criterion on which both attempts score at or above the typical student no
longer discriminates in unsupervised conditions. A criterion on which they
score below it still does, and the last column records why.

## Decision
- [ ] Keep / modify (state how) / move to supervised conditions
- [ ] If modified: the change checked against the deadline for module
      amendments
- [ ] Result and decision entered in the decisions log of the instruction file
- [ ] Rerun planned for next year: [date]
```

### G. A written standard as a skill {#tpl-g}

Save as `.claude/skills/lecture-style/SKILL.md`, with more pairs of examples in `examples.md` in the same folder (a placeholder version is in the repository's `templates/` folder). The rules shown are placeholders, to be replaced with your own (chapter 13).

```text
---
name: lecture-style
description: House style for lecture notes and slides in my modules. Use when writing or reviewing any teaching material.
---

## Rules
1. One idea per slide. A slide has a title that states the point, not the topic.
2. Paragraphs in notes are at most four sentences.
3. Every equation that is used later is numbered; no others are.
4. A new symbol is defined in the sentence where it first appears.
5. Each result is followed by one sentence of interpretation in plain words.
6. Worked examples use real data and state the source and sample period.

## Do not
- Open a section by announcing what it will do.
- Use rhetorical questions as slide titles.
- Use: "it is important to note", "delve", "crucial", "in today's world".

## Examples
Breaks rule 1:   title "Fama-MacBeth regressions"
Corrected:       title "Fama-MacBeth: estimate the price of risk period by period"
(more pairs in examples.md)

## When reviewing
Do not rewrite. Report each finding as:
  file and location | rule number | what is wrong | suggested fix
Finish with a count of findings per rule.
```

### H. Assessment loop: setter, candidate, examiner {#tpl-h}

Three files make up the system in chapter 15. You start only the skill, with `/assessment-loop assessment/coursework1`; the session that runs it acts as the setter and calls the candidate and examiner subagents in each round. The assessment folder needs a `student/` subfolder with exactly what students receive and a `marking/` subfolder with `rubric.md`. The system is untested, so run it first on a short problem set with a round limit of two.

Save as `.claude/agents/candidate.md`:

```text
---
name: candidate
description: Attempts an assessment exactly as a student would, from the student-facing files only. Called by the assessment-loop skill.
omitClaudeMd: true
---

You are a student taking this module. You are given the full path of a
folder that holds the assessment brief and any data. Read only the files in
that folder.

Complete the assessment in full and save your submission in that folder, in
the format the brief asks for. Work as a capable student would with the tools
available: write and run code where needed, and check your own work once
before submitting.

Do not look for a rubric, marking notes, solutions or earlier attempts, and
do not open any file outside the folder. Do not ask questions.
When finished, reply with the name of your submission file and a list of any
wording you found ambiguous.
```

Save as `.claude/agents/examiner.md`:

```text
---
name: examiner
description: Marks one anonymous submission against a rubric, criterion by criterion. Called by the assessment-loop skill.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob
---

You are marking one anonymous submission. You are given the full path of the
submission and of the rubric. Read nothing else, and assume nothing about who
wrote the submission.

For each criterion give a mark, the band, and one sentence quoting or
pointing to the evidence in the submission. You cannot run code: check each
reported number against the code output saved with the submission, list any
number you cannot confirm this way, and do not award marks for it.

Reply with a table (criterion | mark | band | evidence), then the total, the
two criteria on which the submission was strongest, and any place where the
rubric gave you no guidance. Do not edit files or run code.
```

Save as `.claude/skills/assessment-loop/SKILL.md`. Run with `/assessment-loop assessment/coursework1`.

```text
---
name: assessment-loop
description: Tests an assessment by having a candidate subagent sit it and an examiner subagent mark it, and revises it until a stopping rule is met.
disable-model-invocation: true
argument-hint: "[assessment folder, e.g. assessment/coursework1]"
---

You are the setter for the assessment in $ARGUMENTS, and you run the loop.
In each round you call the candidate and examiner subagents yourself. The
lecturer starts you and approves the plan, and does not call the subagents.

Settings (edit before running):
  stop when the candidate's total is below 50, or after 3 rounds,
  or when no revision satisfies the constraints.

The assessment folder must contain:
  student/   exactly what a student receives: brief, data, reading list
  marking/   rubric.md, and any marking notes or model answers

Constraints on every revision:
  - every learning outcome in CLAUDE.md that the original assessed is still assessed
  - format, weighting, word limit and time allowance unchanged
  - a well-prepared student can complete it using only what the module taught
  - no trick wording and no reliance on information students cannot obtain

Before round 1:
  1. Check that student/ and marking/ exist and list their files. If either
     is missing or empty, stop and say what is needed.
  2. Check that .claude/agents/ contains candidate.md and examiner.md.
  3. Copy student/ and marking/ unchanged to versions/v0/.
  4. Show me the files, the settings and the constraints, and wait for my
     approval.

Round N, starting at 1, uses the latest version vK:
  1. Copy versions/vK/student/ to rounds/roundN/student/.
  2. Use the candidate subagent. Give it the full path of
     rounds/roundN/student/ and nothing else about the assessment. It saves
     its submission in that folder.
  3. Use the examiner subagent. Give it the full paths of the submission and
     of versions/vK/marking/rubric.md. Save its report to
     rounds/roundN/report.md.
  4. Add the marks by criterion for this round to rounds/summary.md.
  5. Check the stopping rule. If it is met, go to the final report.
  6. Identify the criteria the candidate passed most easily. Propose one or
     two revisions that satisfy every constraint, and record each in
     changes.md with the criterion it targets and the reason.
  7. Write the revised student/ and marking/ folders to the next version,
     versions/v(K+1)/, and start the next round.

Final report (report.md): the original and final versions side by side, the
change log, marks by criterion for every round, the final attempt in full,
and which constraints came under strain. State plainly if the format could
not be made robust.

Never edit student/ or marking/ in the assessment folder; work on copies.
Never give the candidate the marking files, the change log or earlier rounds.
```

### I. Skill skeleton {#tpl-i}

The parts of a skill from chapter 12, to fill in. Save as `SKILL.md` in a folder named after the task: `.claude/skills/<name>/` in Claude Code.

```text
---
name: task-name
description: What the skill does and when to use it. Put the main use first, in the words a colleague would use to ask for it.
---

[One line stating the task. In Claude Code, $ARGUMENTS stands for what is
typed after the skill's name, for example the week.]

Inputs
- [file or folder]: [what it is]
- If an input is missing, stop and list what is missing. Do not supply it.

Steps
1. ...
2. [a check from chapter 9, written as a step]
3. ...

Output
- [files, and where they go]
- A report: what was produced, what was verified and how, and anything
  that could not be verified.

Do not
- [what the agent must not do]

Supporting files, read only when needed
- [rubric.md]: [when to read it]

Owner: [name]. Last tested: [date], on [module].
Changes:
- [date] [what changed and why]
```

### J. Annual update {#tpl-j}

The year-to-year update from chapter 5. Save as `.claude/skills/annual-update/SKILL.md`. Run with `/annual-update 2027-28`.

```text
---
name: annual-update
description: Prepare the module for a new academic year. Finds dated material, reruns figure and solution scripts on current data, and reports every change against last year. Use once a year before teaching starts.
disable-model-invocation: true
argument-hint: "[academic year, e.g. 2027-28]"
---

Prepare the module for the academic year $ARGUMENTS.

1. Read CLAUDE.md, including the decisions log.
2. List everything that has dated, with file and location: data ending in
   an old year, superseded references, examples overtaken by events, dates
   and deadlines in admin/. Change nothing yet.
3. Wait for me to mark which items to update.
4. If the folder is under version control, commit its current state first.
5. Rerun every figure and solution script on current data. Record the
   download date of each dataset next to it.
6. Where a rerun changes a number in the notes, slides or solutions, take
   the new number from the output and list the change.
7. Make the other approved updates.
8. Compile or run every changed file and fix any errors.
9. Report: each change against last year's version, file by file; every
   number that changed, old and new; anything you could not update.

Never edit sources/. Do not change learning outcomes or assessment
weightings: list any that look out of date for me to raise at module review.
```

### K. Notebook release {#tpl-k}

The release checks from chapter 6, with the mechanical part in a script (chapter 12). Save as `.claude/skills/notebook-release/SKILL.md`, with the script `scripts/release.py` from the repository's `templates/` folder in the same skill folder. Mark solution cells with the tag `solution` in Jupyter. The script needs Jupyter installed in the module's environment. Run with `/notebook-release problem-sets/ps3/ps3.ipynb`.

```text
---
name: notebook-release
description: Check that a solution notebook runs from top to bottom and produce the student version without the solution cells. Use before releasing any notebook to students.
disable-model-invocation: true
argument-hint: "[path to the solution notebook]"
allowed-tools: Bash(${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/release.py *)
---

Release the notebook $ARGUMENTS.

1. Check that the installed package versions match the pinned versions in
   the module (requirements.txt or its equivalent in CLAUDE.md). Report any
   difference and stop.
2. Run ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/release.py on the notebook. The script
   runs the notebook in a fresh kernel and stops at the first error. If it
   ran, it writes NAME-student.ipynb next to it, without the cells tagged
   "solution" and with all outputs cleared.
3. If the run fails, report the cell and the error. Do not edit the
   notebook to make it pass without telling me exactly what you changed.
4. Read the student version. Check that every question still makes sense
   without the removed cells, and that no answer survives in a markdown cell
   or a comment.
5. Report: whether the notebook ran and how long it took, which cells were
   removed, and anything in the student version that needs my attention.

Never release a student version from a notebook that did not run.
```

### L. Test cases for a skill {#tpl-l}

The test file from chapter 12, filled in for template B. Save as `tests.md` in the skill's folder, and do not mention it in `SKILL.md`.

```text
# Test cases for the problem-set skill

Not read in normal use: SKILL.md does not point to this file. Run each case
in a fresh session after any edit to the skill and after each update to the
tool or model, and record the result below.

## Case 1: empirical questions with data
Input: /problem-set week05, with lecture notes for week 5 and a dataset in data/.
A correct output:
- every number in solutions.tex appears in the output of solve.py
- the checker ran, and its disagreements are listed (or it found none)
- the report lists the stretch questions
- no question reproduces or paraphrases an exercise from sources/

## Case 2: derivations only
Input: /problem-set week07, a week whose material is derivations with no data.
A correct output:
- each final expression is verified symbolically or numerically, and the
  report says how
- solve.py contains the verification, not an empty placeholder
- the checker and report items from case 1

## Case 3: missing input
Input: /problem-set week11, with no lecture notes for week 11.
A correct output:
- the skill stops and lists what is missing; no files are written

## Requests that should start the skill
- "Write next week's problem set"
- "I need exercises with solutions for week 6"

## Requests that should not
- "Mark these problem-set answers"
- "Fix the typo in question 3 of ps5"

## Results

| Date | Tool and model | Case 1 | Case 2 | Case 3 | Trigger | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
```

### M. Module `.gitignore` {#tpl-m}

The material chapter 4 keeps out of a repository. Save as `.gitignore` at the top of the module folder, and adjust the folder names to your own layout. The module template in the repository already contains it.

```text
# Material that must never be recorded (chapter 4)
assessment/
sources/third-party/
data/licensed/
admin/students/
*.env
.env

# Files the computer generates
.DS_Store
.ipynb_checkpoints/
__pycache__/
*.aux
*.log
*.out
*.toc
*.nav
*.snm
*.fls
*.fdb_latexmk
*.synctex.gz

# Personal agent settings
.claude/settings.local.json
```

### N. First commit {#tpl-n}

A prompt that puts a module folder under version control (chapter 4), with a check of what goes in before anything is recorded.

```text
This folder is a teaching module that is not yet under version control.

1. Check that Git is installed and tell me which version. If it is not
   installed, stop and tell me how to install it on this computer. Do not
   install it yourself.
2. If there is no .gitignore file, create one from the module template's
   .gitignore and show it to me.
3. List every file the first commit would include, grouped by folder.
   Flag anything that looks like student work, marks, an unreleased exam,
   licensed data, or a password or key. Wait for my approval.
4. Initialise the repository and make the first commit, with the message
   "Module as of [today's date]".
5. Explain briefly what you did and how I can undo a change later.

Do not create a GitHub repository and do not push anything. I will do that
myself.
```

### O. Checks on every change {#tpl-o}

The GitHub Actions workflow from chapter 14. It compiles every LaTeX document and runs every notebook in `lectures/` and `problem-sets/`, and needs a `requirements.txt` listing the module's Python packages. Save as `.github/workflows/module-checks.yml`.

```yaml
# Save as .github/workflows/module-checks.yml in the module repository.
# On every push to main and every pull request, it compiles each LaTeX file
# that contains \documentclass and runs each notebook from top to bottom,
# in lectures/ and problem-sets/. Untested on a live module. If GitHub
# reports an action version below as out of date, update it.
name: Module checks

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  latex:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Install LaTeX
        run: |
          sudo apt-get update
          sudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
            texlive-latex-recommended texlive-latex-extra \
            texlive-fonts-recommended latexmk
      - name: Compile every document
        run: |
          status=0
          while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do
            grep -q '\\documentclass' "$f" || continue
            echo "::group::$f"
            if ! (cd "$(dirname "$f")" && latexmk -pdf -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error "$(basename "$f")"); then
              echo "::error file=$f::did not compile"
              status=1
            fi
            echo "::endgroup::"
          done < <(find lectures problem-sets -name '*.tex' -print0 2>/dev/null)
          exit $status

  notebooks:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - name: Install the pinned packages
        run: |
          if [ -f requirements.txt ]; then pip install -r requirements.txt; fi
          pip install nbconvert ipykernel
      - name: Run every notebook from top to bottom
        run: |
          status=0
          while IFS= read -r -d '' nb; do
            echo "::group::$nb"
            if ! jupyter nbconvert --to notebook --execute --output-dir "$RUNNER_TEMP/executed" "$nb"; then
              echo "::error file=$nb::did not run"
              status=1
            fi
            echo "::endgroup::"
          done < <(find lectures problem-sets -name '*.ipynb' -not -name '*-student.ipynb' -not -path '*/.ipynb_checkpoints/*' -print0 2>/dev/null)
          exit $status
```

### P. A hook that protects `sources/` {#tpl-p}

The hook from chapter 14, for Claude Code. Save the script as `.claude/hooks/protect-sources.py` (it is in the repository's `templates/` folder), and add the settings below to `.claude/settings.json`. The deny rule covers the editing tools and the shell commands Claude Code recognises, and the hook gives the agent a clear reason when it blocks an edit. Neither stops a script the agent runs from writing into the folder, so make `sources/` read-only on your computer as well.

```json
{
  "permissions": {
    "deny": ["Edit(/sources/**)"]
  },
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Edit|Write|NotebookEdit",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "python3 \"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR\"/.claude/hooks/protect-sources.py"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```
